Segment: Historical Evolution, goal pre-computer early-era developments anticipated immersive VR. Sentences:
[1] Now, let us talk about the early era.
[2] So, whenever I use the term virtual reality, we immediately associate it with some devices that that are computer in nature.
[3] So, essentially it is difficult for us to think of virtual reality without thinking of computers, particularly computer displays.
[4] However, you will be surprised to know that the concept in some form existed even before computers were officially developed in the 1940s, before the advent of modern digital computers in the 1940s.
[5] So, of course, not everything was there, but a few things conceptually were similar to what we consider to be immersive experience in virtual reality.
[6] There are a few key developments in this era we can roughly associate with virtual reality experience.
[7] The first of those was developed in 1838 by Sir Charles Wheatstone, who demonstrated a stereoscopic device and established for the first time in recorded history that our brain can process 2D images as 3D objects.
[8] So, this can be roughly considered to be the first step toward creation of immersive experience.
[9] Remember that when we experience virtual reality, we wear either headsets or experience it through some display devices.
[10] Each display device is 2D in nature, but due to our stereoscopic vision, we see these images together in the form of 3D objects, 3D space.

[1] With this knowledge, let us now come back to our original case study that is Majuli VR Tour Design.
[2] So, here the first stage is, of course, as we discussed: requirement gathering, gathering usability requirements for the users, for the tour.
[3] So, earlier we talked about the basic idea of usability requirement gathering, also how to analyze and specify.
[4] For analysis, we talked about the affinity diagram method; for specification, we talked about functional specification.
[5] Now, let us try to understand this knowledge, how it can be useful in the context of the Majuli VR Tour.
[6] So, in order to identify the requirements, what we did is we made several field trips to Majuli, interviewed people, observed people in their natural work settings, and collected the data.
[7] The data that we discussed earlier, which is in terms of notes, we collected data.
[8] One thing to be noted here is that the system is not necessarily meant for only the people who are residing on Majuli.
[9] In fact, they are least likely to use it because they are already there.
[10] It is meant to be used by those not residing on the island.
[11] So, we have to keep that in mind.
[12] Our users are not necessarily those who are on the island, but rather those who are not on the island.
[13] So, through the field trips, interviews, and observations, we have identified three potential user groups who would be interested in experiencing the VR tour.
[14] One group would be students or learners, those with an interest in knowing about the island.
[15] Another group would be tourists.
[16] They are interested in exploring tourist spots or other interesting places on the island.
[17] And thirdly, pilgrims who are interested in the religious practices, those who are interested in the religious places and in the religious practices.
[18] So, we have identified these three groups: students or learners, tourists and pilgrims based on our interactions and observations. during the field trips.
[19] So, after interacting with people, we got this idea and utilized their experience about the visitors who come to the islands, what they typically do, who comes, what they typically do, these types of information we obtained after interacting with the people there on the island and based on that we have identified these three groups.
[20] So, that is the first stage, that is know the user.
[21] So, we are targeting a usable system that is Majuli VR Tour meant for these three categories of users.
[22] Note that we are not claiming that our system will be usable to anybody in any work context for any task.
[23] We are assuming that it will be usable only for these three groups of users.
[24] Then, once the user groups were identified, we conducted contextual inquiry on the chosen user group samples, from the user groups to learn about their needs and expectations from the system, which helped us identify the system features to be supported for each group so that the system is usable for each group of users.
[25] So through this process, we managed to address a few key design challenges.
[26] Key challenges that we have listed out earlier.
[27] What are those challenges?
[28] So, coverage of large geographical area, we have large multimodal data to provide comprehensive view because the nature of the data and geographical area is huge.
[29] It is time consuming to explore the entire island with all the data that we have collected which may lead to cyber sickness.
[30] So, how to avoid cyber sickness was one of the key challenges which we could address following the requirement gathering method.
[31] So, essentially how did we address the challenge?

[1] We can sometimes have indirect manipulation where we are not directly manipulating using our physical hand.
[2] Instead, we are manipulating some other objects which in turn are manipulating the desired object.
[3] So, these other objects are mapped to the desired virtual object and by manipulating the other objects, we are essentially manipulating the desired objects.
[4] This is called indirect manipulation.
[5] It allows users to manipulate virtual objects without directly interacting with the virtual object.
[6] Instead, the user interacts with some other objects that are mapped to the virtual objects.
[7] A simple way of doing this is using the 3D widgets.
[8] So, we are already familiar with such widgets.
[9] For example, if I want to scroll up or down a page, I can directly do so or I can use a scroll bar to do so.
[10] Now, usage of a scroll bar is essentially an indirect way of manipulating the interface.
[11] So, here I am not directly moving the page up or down; instead I am moving the scroll bar up and down and correspondingly the page is moving up and down.
[12] So, that is an example of a 2D widget.
[13] Similarly, we can have 3D widgets in the virtual world by manipulating the 3D widgets; widgets and handles are there to put controls directly in the 3D scene with the objects.
[14] Typically, each widget is responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom.
[15] So, for a given object, a single widget may not be sufficient to manipulate all properties.
[16] Instead, for a specified set of degrees of freedom can be manipulated using 3D widgets, using each widget.
[17] Another indirect manipulation technique is through the use of indirect proxies.
[18] It allows users a more natural grasping method to perform direct manipulation through local proxies.
[19] For example, this physical proxy prop is used to control the orientation of a neurological data set.

1 Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.
2 Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.
3 Wayfinding is essentially a mental model, and the goal of wayfinding is to build a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment so that it is easier to locate oneself and identify a suitable path.

11 Breadcrumb support for wayfinding leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.
12 A compass or another direction indicator can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space, and a compass can be designed and placed in the environment.

[1] Previously, we talked about how to evaluate the usability of our designs, whatever designs we have come up with.

[5] So, everything that we talked about was on a very limited scale.
[6] Be it expert evaluation or user evaluation.
[7] That limited scale, of course, is good enough for quickly identifying some major usability issues that may be there in our design.
[8] Now, the idea of the design-prototype-evaluate lifecycle is to have a quick design, get a quick prototype, and get a quick evaluation of the prototype so that we identify the issues.
[9] Then we rectify the design again, rectify the prototype, perform another quick evaluation, and so on, until the number of problems reduces.
[10] Now, in order to make it quick, to make everything quick, what we do is basically employ a limited number of evaluators and do the evaluation only on prototypes.
[11] This is, of course, good for early evaluation.
[12] However, it cannot give us a conclusive result about the overall usability of the end system.
[13] For that, we need to evaluate our whole implemented system with a larger number of users, preferably, to get a conclusive idea on usability.
[14] Now, in order to get that conclusive idea on usability, what we need is a fully implemented system.
[15] It cannot be done on prototypes.
[16] The second thing is, in order to do that, what we generally need to do is perform a controlled experiment to collect user behavioral data and also to analyze that data, to come to a conclusion.
[17] So, two things are important: one is a fully implemented system, and second is a controlled experiment.
[18] So, these two we must have access to or we must execute to be able to perform or to be able to conclude about the usability of the overall system.
[19] Now, when we talk about such controlled experiments, generally that is referred to as empirical research or an empirical study or a user study.
[20] However, in our context, it is specifically related to usability evaluation.
